findings.problem: cancel_download accepts only {200, 202, 204}. Any other non-5xx status, including 404 for a transfer slskd has already finished or removed, falls through to the generic branch at line 260. That branch raises TransferEnqueueError(reason='unavailable') with the message 'slskd transfer request failed'. A cancel that races a transfer finishing, or a second cancel of the same item, therefore looks like the service is down instead of a cancel that needs no further work. No production caller exists yet, so this assumes the planned caller (22-RESEARCH.md:154) does not treat 404 as success. pending: confirm how slskd answers DELETE for an unknown or completed id and how the future cancel caller handles 'unavailable'.
findings.title: Cancelling a transfer slskd already removed (404) raises a generic 'unavailable' error instead of succeeding
findings.why_it_matters: A user who cancels an item that just finished could see a spurious 'slskd unavailable' failure, and retry logic keyed on 'unavailable' could keep re-sending a cancel that can never succeed.

agent_notes: The change only adds to the API. cancel_download is a new public method. success_statuses is a new keyword-only parameter on the private _request_json, and it defaults to None, which falls back to {200, 201}. Every existing _request_json caller in transfer.py behaves exactly as before.

Callers of transfer.py: cli.py, pipeline.py, web/pipeline_runner.py and scripts/m001_live_proof.py. None of them call cancel_download yet, and none pass success_statuses, so the existing enqueue and poll paths are unaffected.
`success_statuses or {200, 201}` would turn an explicit empty set into the default instead of 'accept nothing'. No caller passes an empty set, so this has no effect today.

A 204 or other empty body is handled by the existing `if not response.content: return {}` at transfer.py:266, so a 204 from DELETE returns {} correctly. A non-dict JSON body is turned into {} by the isinstance guard in cancel_download.

Security: username and transfer_id are both percent-encoded with safe='', so '/' and '..' cannot reach other slskd paths, and tests/test_transfer.py:292 covers this. The rules that keep the API key out of logs and handle 401/403, 429 and 5xx are reused unchanged.
Naming: cancel failures are raised as TransferEnqueueError. That works, but downstream handlers or logs that key on the class name will label cancel errors as enqueue errors.
No database, schema, migration or performance impact. It is one HTTP DELETE per cancel, reusing the existing client and timeout.
Blast radius: limited to transfer.py, and nothing in production calls the new method yet. The only real risk is how the upcoming cancel orchestration handles the 404 and race cases.
Verdict: shippable as-is. There is one non-blocking note about how 404 is classified on cancel.

findings.problem: cancel_download only accepts {200, 202, 204} (line 212). A transfer that finished, failed or was removed between the job snapshot and the cancel request gets a 404 from slskd. _request_json then raises TransferEnqueueError('slskd transfer request failed with HTTP 404', 'unavailable') at lines 260-264. The 'unavailable' reason is the same one used for real outages, so a caller cannot tell a no-op cancel apart from slskd being down.
